newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Soft EMU option grows despite calls for austerity.
newsitem.headline: Soft EMU option grows despite calls for austerity.

text.p: Senior European policy-makers on Tuesday urged governments to whip their budgets into shape ahead of the euro's introduction in January 1999 but left open how much belt-tightening would actually be needed to join.

Bank of France chief Jean-Claude Trichet, presenting the Bank's annual report in Paris, said it was essential that the French government make further cuts in its 1997 budget, the critical year in which countries will be judged on their qualifications for economic and monetary union (EMU).

"Reducing public deficits is indispensable in 1997 as it is in the medium term," Trichet told a news conference, adding that his report was written before the new Socialist government announced its policy programme last week.
Trichet called for continuing wage restraint and said France's payroll deductions to fund the country's welfare system were too high.
In a separate interview with the Paris daily Le Monde, Trichet said it would be "unthinkable" for certain governments not to take corrective action on the budgets.

Doubts over the ability of countries like France to meet the budgetary demands of EMU have grown in recent weeks due to the new government's emphasis on jobs and growth and solemn pledges not to engage in more austerity measures.

The leftward political lurch in France along with the struggle Germany and others are having in putting their public finances in order have raised expectations of a broad membership in EMU, what many now call the soft euro option.

For EMU to start on time with budget deficits in some of the EU's larger economies above three percent of GDP -- the Maastricht Treaty's target -- a more generous reading of the deficit criterion would have to be applied by EU leaders when they decide on the founding members in the spring of 1998.
EU Monetary Affairs Commissioner Yves-Thibault de Silguy fuelled speculation that such an interpretation would indeed be necessary in comments he made on Tuesday in reference to the French situation.

"It's not a question of applying too brutally and simply the figure of three percent," his spokesman, Patrick Child, quoted him as telling Italian journalists. "It's necessary to look at all of the treaty conditions and the text that surrounds it."
However, at the same time he stressed the need to protect the euro's credibility.
"There is a small margin of manoeuvre but we should not take risks with the credibility of the euro."
He also said there was no reason to fear that France, seen as an indispensable member of EMU, would not be ready to take part in the single currency's launch.

The most vocal advocate of a strict reading of the euro's entry rules has been Germany. But even in a country long seen as a paragon of fiscal virtue, the combined force of the government's poor finances and the political imperatives of EMU have prompted a noticeable re-evaluation.
Those benefiting the most from the soft-euro scenario are southern European countries like Italy, which is expected to see its budget deficit climb well above the three percent threshold.
Europe's fledgling central bank issued a bond priced in lira which can be redenominated into euros once the new currency is launched - showing it believes Italy could make the grade for membership.

The Italian industrialists group, Confindustria, said in a report on Tuesday that Rome's deficit was on course to come in at around 3.4 percent of GDP, but it said it expected the government to introduce further budget cuts this year.

Italian Finance Minister Vincenzo Visco told a convention in Rome that the government had tamed the once-tearaway public deficit, had inflation under control and was expecting economic output to recover rapidly from a weak first quarter.
Spain's central bank governor Luis Angel Rojo, whose country is widely seen as a front-runner in the euro race, voiced optimism over his country's chances of making the EMU grade.

In an address accompanying the Bank's annual report, Rojo said policies oriented toward greater stability of the Spanish economy have "strongly raised the probability that Spain joins European economic and monetary union from the first moment."
